x_to_y: This edge represents a direct causal effect of \(x\) on \(y\): changing \(x\) (through policy, price, treatment intensity, or another intervention) shifts the outcome \(y\) holding other determinants fixed. The main threats are confounding (unobserved factors affecting both \(x\) and \(y\)), reverse causality if \(y\) also affects \(x\), and measurement error in \(x\) that can attenuate or distort the estimated effect. Next, the researcher should articulate a credible identification strategy (e.g., randomized variation, IV, diff-in-diff, RD), check pre-trends/balance or instrument validity as applicable, and probe robustness to alternative controls/specifications and placebo or falsification tests.
y_to_z: This edge encodes a causal effect of \(y\) on \(z\): changes in \(y\) directly shift \(z\) through whatever behavioral, technological, or institutional mechanism links the two (e.g., \(y\) as a policy lever or input and \(z\) as an outcome). The main threats are reverse causality (if \(z\) also affects \(y\)), omitted common causes of \(y\) and \(z\) that induce spurious correlation, and measurement error in \(y\) that can attenuate estimates or create bias if correlated with unobservables. Next, the researcher should articulate the concrete mechanism and timing (does \(y\) move before \(z\)?), assess whether any backdoor paths remain open in the DAG, and look for a credible source of exogenous variation in \(y\) (or a valid set of controls/IV) to support identification.
